ref: Leg. 10 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 19-21]
greek: ἀγγέλων καὶ λειτουργῶν φαμεν, οὓς ὁ ποιητὴς καὶ δημιουργὸς κόσμον θεὸς διὰ τοῦ παρ᾽ αὐτοῦ λόγου διένειμε καὶ διέταξε περὶ τε τὰ στοιχεῖα εἶναι καὶ τοὺς οὐρανοὺς καὶ τὸν κόσμον καὶ τὰ ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν τούτων εὐταξίαν.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated; p.50 line 1 image-checked, first words from OCR
english: but we recognise also a multitude of angels and ministers, whom God the Maker and Framer of the world distributed and appointed to their several posts by His Logos, to occupy themselves about the elements, and the heavens, and the world, and the things in it, and the goodly ordering of them all.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: God the Maker and Framer distributed angels and ministers through his Logos, to order the elements, heavens and world.
limits: Objection it answers: the Logos is one of the angels or a creature. The sentence places the Logos as the agent through whom God orders the angels, not as one of them. It does not state the Logos's generation. First word of the phrase 'δημιουργὸς κόσμον' is OCR (the article before κόσμον is not legible); p.50 line 1 checked on image.

ref: Leg. 10 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 15-18]
greek: Τίς οὖν οὐκ ἂν ἀπορήσαι, λέγοντας θεὸν πατέρα καὶ υἱὸν θεὸν καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, δεικνύντας αὐτῶν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ ἑνώσει δύναμιν καὶ τὴν ἐν τῇ τάξει διαίρεσιν, ἀκούσας ἀθέους καλουμένους;
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: Who, then, would not be astonished to hear men who speak of God the Father, and of God the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and who declare both their power in union and their distinction in order, called atheists?
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: Those who name God the Father, God the Son and the Holy Spirit, and show their power in union and distinction in order, are wrongly called atheists.
limits: Shows three named divine persons with 'power in union' and 'distinction in order'. No word for Trinity (τριάς) and no 'homoousios'. Otto's note 16 records a Paris MS variant that places a stop after υἱόν, so that 'θεόν' refers to the Holy Spirit (the Spirit as God). Otto suspects an emendation ἐν δυνάμει ἕνωσιν (Venema), which he discusses and rejects.

ref: Leg. 10 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 14-17]
greek: Καίτοι καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ ἐνεργοῦν τοῖς ἐκφωνοῦσι προφητικῶς ἅγιον πνεῦμα ἀπόῤῥοιαν εἶναί φαμεν τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀποῤῥέον καὶ ἐπαναφερόμενον ὡς ἀκτῖνα ἡλίου.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: The Holy Spirit Himself also, which operates in the prophets, we assert to be an effluence of God, flowing from Him, and returning back again like a beam of the sun.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: The Spirit that works in the prophets is called an effluence (ἀπόῤῥοια) of God, flowing out and returning like a sunbeam.
limits: Objection: the Spirit is only a power or emanation, not a person. The text calls the Spirit 'acting' (ἐνεργοῦν) but uses the impersonal image of an effluence, and does not say 'person' or 'God'. Otto notes a variant order (Lub.: ἀπόῤῥοιαν φαμὲν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι). Note: the Spirit is named as the agent in prophecy here.

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 5-7]
greek: Ὡς γὰρ θεὸν φαμεν καὶ υἱὸν τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ καὶ πνεῦμα ἅγιον, ἑνούμενα μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν τὸν πατέρα τὸν υἱὸν τὸ πνεῦμα, ὅτι νοῦς λόγος σοφία ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ πατρός, καὶ ἀπόῤῥοια ὡς φῶς ἀπὸ πυρὸς τὸ πνεῦμα, οὕτως καὶ ἑτέρας εἶναι δυνάμεις κατειλήμμεθα περὶ τὴν ὕλην ἀρχούσας καὶ δι᾽ αὐτῆς,
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: For, as we acknowledge a God, and a Son his Logos, and a Holy Spirit, united in essence — the Father, the Son, the Spirit, because the Son is the Intelligence, Reason, Wisdom of the Father, and the Spirit an effluence, as light from fire; so also do we apprehend the existence of other powers, which exercise dominion about matter, and by means of it, and one in particular, which is hostile to God:
page: Otto p. 124 (Greek); note 6 on Latin p. 125
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: Father, Son (Logos) and Holy Spirit are named together; the Son is 'Intelligence, Reason, Wisdom' of the Father and the Spirit an effluence like light from fire; other 'powers' act about matter.
limits: Shows the Son as Logos-Nous-Sophia of the Father, and the Spirit as effluence (ἀπόῤῥοια). But Otto's printed Greek says 'united in POWER' (κατὰ δύναμιν), not 'united in essence'. ANF's 'united in essence' follows Gesner's rejected conjecture (see A5-12). Also: 'τρία' does not appear in the printed text. Other powers (ἑτέρας δυνάμεις) are placed about matter, so the same Greek sentence names the Son and the Spirit among 'powers'.

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 1-7 of the end of ch. 24]
greek: μὲν γὰρ ἄλλοι, αὐθαίρετοι δὴ οἷοι γεγόνασιν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, ἔμειναν ἐφ᾽ οἷς αὐτοὺς ἐποίησεν καὶ διέταξεν ὁ θεός, οἱ δὲ ἐνύβρισαν καὶ τῇ τῆς οὐσίας ὑποστάσει καὶ τῇ ἀρχῇ, οὗτός τε ὁ τῆς ὕλης καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῇ εἰδῶν ἄρχων καὶ ἕτεροι τῶν περὶ τὸ πρῶτον τοῦτο στερέωμα, ἐκεῖνοι μὲν εἰς ἐπιθυμίαν πεσόντες παρθένων καὶ ἥττους σαρκὸς εὑρεθέντες, οὗτος δὲ ἀμελήσας καὶ πονηρὸς περὶ τὴν τῶν πεπιστευμένων γενόμενος διοίκησιν. Ἐκ μὲν οὖν τῶν περὶ τὰς παρθένους ἐχόντων οἱ καλούμενοι ἐγεννήθησαν γίγαντες.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated; image p.130 viewed; the first word (μὲν γὰρ) continues from p.128
english: Just as with men, who have freedom of choice as to both virtue and vice (for you would not either honour the good or punish the bad, unless vice and virtue were in their own power; and some are diligent in the matters entrusted to them by you, and others faithless), so is it among the angels. Some, free agents, you will observe, such as they were created by God, continued in those things for which God had made and over which He had ordained them; but some outraged both the constitution of their nature and the government entrusted to them: namely, this ruler of matter and its various forms, and others of those who were placed about this first firmament (you know that we say nothing without witnesses, but state the things which have been declared by the prophets); these fell into impure love of virgins, and were subjugated by the flesh, and he became negligent and wicked in the management of the things entrusted to him. Of these lovers of virgins, therefore, were begotten those who are called giants.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: Some angels kept their station; others (the prince of matter and some of his companions) outraged their nature and their charge; the 'lovers of virgins' produced the giants.
limits: Objection: the 'prince of matter' is a rival power to God (dualism). The Greek says he was created by God (ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, see A5-07) and fell by misuse of a delegated charge. Otto notes 'Sic etiam c. 24 (bis) vocatur' for the title. Heavy angelology: no word about the Son or Spirit here.

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 18-21]
greek: Τοῦτο γὰρ ἡ τῶν ἀγγέλων σύστασις, τῷ θεῷ ἐπὶ προνοίᾳ γεγονέναι τοῖς ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ διακεκοσμημένοις, ἵνα τὴν μὲν παντελικὴν καὶ γενικὴν ὁ θεὸς ἔχῃ τῶν ὅλων πρόνοιαν, τὴν δὲ ἐπὶ μέρους οἱ ἐπ᾽ αὐτοῖς ταχθέντες ἄγγελοι.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: For this is the office of the angels — to exercise providence for God over the things created and ordered by Him; so that God may have the universal and general providence of the whole, while the particular parts are provided for by the angels appointed over them.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: The angels exist to exercise particular providence for God; God keeps the universal providence.
limits: Answers the charge that the gods and angels rival God's providence: God keeps universal providence, angels only the particulars. Otto's note 20 cites Epiphanius/Methodius-type readings and proposes variant γέγονέν; the printed text stands. No Logos or Spirit named in this sentence.

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 14-19]
greek: μίαν μὲν τὴν ἀντίθεον, οὐχ ὅτι ἀντιδοξοῦν τί ἐστι τῷ θεῷ, ὡς τῇ φιλίᾳ τὸ νεῖκος κατὰ τὸν Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ τῇ ἡμέρα νὺξ κατὰ τὰ φαινόμενα, […] ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι τῷ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγαθῷ, ὃ κατὰ συμβεβηκὸς ἐστιν αὐτῷ καὶ συνυπάρχον, ὡς χρόα σώματι, […] ἐναντίον ἐστὶ τὸ περὶ τὴν ὕλην ἔχον πνεῦμα, γενόμενον μὲν ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ, καθὸ οἱ λοιποὶ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ γεγόνασιν ἄγγελοι, καὶ τὴν ἐπὶ τῇ ὕλῃ καὶ τοῖς τῆς ὕλης εἴδεσι πιστευσάμενον διοίκησιν.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: not that anything is really opposed to God, like strife to friendship, according to Empedocles, and night to day, according to the appearing and disappearing of the stars (for even if anything had placed itself in opposition to God, it would have ceased to exist, its structure being destroyed by the power and might of God), but that to the good that is in God, which belongs of necessity to Him, and co-exists with Him, as color with body, without which it has no existence (not as being part of it, but as an attendant property co-existing with it, united and blended, just as it is natural for fire to be yellow and the ether dark blue) — to the good that is in God, I say, the spirit which is about matter, who was created by God, just as the other angels were created by Him, and entrusted with the control of matter and the forms of matter, is opposed.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: The spirit about matter that opposes the good of God was itself created by God like the other angels; opposition is to God's good, not a second principle.
limits: Answers the dualist objection (an evil principle opposed to God). Athenagoras says the opposed spirit was 'made by God'. The brackets mark omitted parenthetical clauses (on Empedocles' strife, and the colour-and-body image). The phrase 'ὡς τῇ φιλίᾳ' reads as 'ὡς' on the image; OCR gave 'αἷς'. The Greek leaves open the spirit's 'fall' (see A5-05).

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [opening]
greek: Τί δὲ δεῖ πρὸς ὑμᾶς πάντα λόγον κεκινηκότας ἢ ποιητῶν μνημονεύειν ἢ καὶ ἑτέρας δόξας ἐξετάζειν, τοσοῦτον εἰπεῖν ἔχοντι· εἰ μὴ καὶ ποιηταὶ καὶ φιλόσοφοι ἕνα μὲν εἶναι ἐπεγινώσκον θεόν, περὶ δὲ τούτων οἱ μὲν ὡς περὶ δαιμόνων, οἱ δὲ ὡς περὶ ὕλης, οἱ δὲ ὡς περὶ ἀνθρώπων γενομένων ἐφρόνουν, ἡμεῖς γε ἂν εἰκότως ἐξενηλατούμεθα, διαιρετικῷ λόγῳ καὶ περὶ θεοῦ καὶ ὕλης καὶ περὶ τῆς τούτων αὐτῶν οὐσίας κεχρημένοι;
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: What need is there, in speaking to you who have searched into every department of knowledge, to mention the poets, or to examine opinions of another kind? Let it suffice to say thus much. If the poets and philosophers did not acknowledge that there is one God, and concerning these gods were not of opinion, some that they are demons, others that they are matter, and others that they once were men, — there might be some show of reason for our being harassed as we are, since we employ language which makes a distinction between God and matter, and the natures of the two.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: Pagan poets and philosophers themselves knew one God and classed the other gods as demons, matter or dead men; Christians are harassed for distinguishing God from matter.
limits: Sets the argument: the charge of atheism is answered by pointing to the pagans' own inconsistency. Says nothing directly about the Son or Spirit. Otto's variants: 'ἐξενηλατούμεθα' (ξενηλατ-) with alternative verb forms in the apparatus (p.125 note 2); printed form kept.

ref: Leg. 25 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [end of chapter]
greek: ὁ δὲ τῆς ὕλης ἄρχων, [ὡς|οἷς] ἔστιν ἐξ αὐτῶν τῶν γινομένων ἰδεῖν, ἐναντία τῷ ἀγαθῷ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπιτροπεύει καὶ διοικεῖ.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: These angels, then, who have fallen from heaven, and haunt the air and the earth, and are no longer able to rise to heavenly things, and the souls of the giants, which are the demons who wander about the world, perform actions similar, the one (that is, the demons) to the natures they have received, the other (that is, the angels) to the appetites they have indulged. But the prince of matter, as may be seen merely from what transpires, exercises a control and management contrary to the good that is in God:
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: The prince of matter visibly governs things against God's good, as observed in events.
limits: Objection: a visible, active ruler of the world opposed to God. Athenagoras frames the 'prince' as a fallen angel's office; the sentence limits the opposition to the sphere of matter and events. Image p.132 read; relative word ὡς (image) vs οἷς (OCR) left in brackets. Otto's note 4 says the title recurs in ch. 24 (bis).

ref: Leg. 26 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [lines 4-6, and the closing sentence]
greek: Οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἀποτέμνουσι τὰ αἰδοῖα, οἱ περὶ τὴν Ῥέαν, οἱ δὲ ἐγκόπτουσιν ἢ ἐντέμνουσιν, οἱ περὶ τὴν Ἄρτεμιν, καὶ ἡ μὲν ἐν Ταύροις φονεύει τοὺς ξένους· […] Ὁ δὲ θεός, τελείως ἀγαθὸς ὢν, ἀϊδίως ἀγαθοποιός ἐστιν.
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: For some castrate, as Rhea; others wound and slaughter, as Artemis; the Tauric goddess puts all strangers to death. I pass over those who lacerate with knives and scourges of bones, and shall not attempt to describe all the kinds of demons; for it is not the part of a god to incite to things against nature. But when the demon plots against a man, He first inflicts some hurt upon his mind. But God, being perfectly good, is eternally doing good.
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: Cult excesses are the work of demons who act through the names of gods; God, being wholly good, does harm to no one.
limits: Answers the claim that the demons are the gods (the pagan gods being men). The middle Greek (omitted, […]) describes further cult cruelties and the verse on demons harming the mind; not transcribed here. Shows only that God is good and the demons are harmful spirits. Nothing about the Son or Spirit.

ref: Leg. 27 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [opening, and lines 4-6 of the first paragraph]
greek: Τί οὖν; Πρῶτα μὲν αἱ τῆς ψυχῆς ἄλογοι καὶ ἰνδαλματώδεις περὶ τὰς δόξας κινήσεις ἄλλοτε ἄλλα εἴδωλα, τὰ μὲν ἀπὸ τῆς ὕλης ἕλκουσι, τὰ δὲ αὐταῖς ἀναπλάττουσι καὶ κυοῦσι. […] ἐναποσφραγίσηται ψευδεῖς περὶ αὐτῆς δόξας, οἱ περὶ τὴν ὕλην δαίμονες, λίχνοι περὶ τὰς κνίσσας καὶ τὸ τῶν ἱερείων αἷμα ὄντες, ἀπατηλοὶ δὲ ἀνθρώπων
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated
english: What then? In the first place, the irrational and fantastic movements of the soul about opinions produce a diversity of images (εἴδωλα) from time to time: some they derive from matter, and some they fashion and bring forth for themselves; and this happens to a soul especially when it partakes of the material spirit and becomes mingled with it, looking not at heavenly things and their Maker, but downwards to earthly things, wholly at the earth, as being now mere flesh and blood, and no longer pure spirit. These irrational and fantastic movements of the soul, then, give birth to empty visions in the mind, by which it becomes madly set on idols. When, too, a tender and susceptible soul, which has no knowledge or experience of sounder doctrines, and is unaccustomed to contemplate truth, and to consider thoughtfully the Father and Maker of all things, gets impressed with false opinions respecting itself, then the demons who hover about matter, greedy of sacrificial odours and the blood of victims, and ever ready to lead men into error, avail themselves of these delusive movements of the souls of the multitude; and, taking possession of their thoughts, cause to flow into the mind empty visions as if coming from the idols and the statues; and when, too, a soul of itself, as being immortal, moves comformably to reason, either predicting the future or healing the present, the demons claim the glory for themselves.
page: Otto p. 142 (opening verified on image); lines to p.142-144
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 2 (ed. Roberts and Donaldson), copy at newadvent.org/fathers/0205.htm; original printing details not checked
what_it_says: False images are produced inside the soul; demons about matter, greedy for sacrifice smoke and blood, impress false opinions and take the glory.
limits: Answers the charge that the Christian demonology is a rival cult: the images are internal and demonic, not the statues themselves. Demons 'about matter' again link to the 'prince of matter'. The OCR of the second clause is less certain than the image of the opening. No Trinitarian content.

ref: Leg. 24 (chapter; Otto and ANF use the same chapter numbers, no section numbers exist; Otto line numbers given in brackets) [note 6 to ch. 24 line 6]
greek: ἑνούμενα μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν (text, p.124) — Gesner's proposal as printed by Otto: τρία μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν, ἑνούμενα δὲ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, τὸν πατέρα
greek_edition: Otto, Corpus Apologetarum Christianorum saeculi secundi vol. VII (Jena: Mauke, 1857); Internet Archive copy corpusapologeta02unkngoog (1969 Sandig reprint), text layer of corpusapologeta02unkngoog_text.pdf, read from OCR and checked on page images where stated; Latin note read on image p.125
english: Frustra Gesnerus, quocum (ut assolet) Rechenbergius facit, legere mallet: τρία μὲν κατὰ δύναμιν, ἑνούμενα δὲ κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, τὸν πατέρα etc. (own translation: Gesner, whom Rechenberg follows as usual, would prefer to read ... ; Otto calls this vain)
translator: Otto (Latin note); own translation of the Latin
page: Otto, Latin commentary p. 125, note 6 on Greek p. 124
what_it_says: Otto (Latin note): Gesner conjectured 'three' (τρία) and 'united in essence' (κατ᾽ οὐσίαν); Otto rejects it and keeps 'united in power'.
limits: This is the key textual point. ANF's 'united in essence' (A5-04) matches Gesner's conjecture, not the printed Greek; the 'three' (τρία) that Gesner wanted is not in the text. Not a manuscript reading. Do not cite τρία as Athenagoras. Whether Pratten followed Gesner or another edition is not checked.
